speechtext: On the orders of the day being called:

I wish to refer to page 6692 of 'Hansard,' April 7. and to call the attention of the House to the following words that occurred in the speech of the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Aylesworth):
There is just one other thing I ought to say in that regard. My hon. friend from South Grey (Mr. Miller) read yesterday a letter I had written to him some two months ago on this subject. I certainly have no objection to his putting the letter on the pages Mr. FRASER.
of ' Hansard ' although I ought to say 1 never expected to see it there, and thought 1 was merely writing to him as one member of the House might write to another what my ideas were with reference to this question.
I shall only occupy probably four minutes of the time of the. House discussing this, and in speaking I am not actuated by any feeling of resentment whatever. I realize that in this matter every man has the right to his own views and I realize quite that those who opposed the Bill had just as good a right to oppose it as I had to vote and work for it. The hon. member for West Northumberland (Mr. McColl), the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster), and the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Sifton) all spoke strongly against the Bill. As far as I am concerned, no feeling of personal friendship will be affected or altered by the action which any man took upon the Bill, nor will I for one moment think of seeking to injure any man politically because he has differed from me in his opinion as to the Bill. While I say that I will not be actuated by any resentment because of any action taken by any other hon. gentleman in what I say; neither will I be restricted in what I say by any party feeling or party affiliation. I do not object to any hon. gentleman differing from me in opinion, but I do like, when I fight a battle, t,o fight it fairly. The Minister of Justice complained that I did a dishonourable thing in making public a letter which it was not intended should be made public. What are the facts? I am sorry that I did not preserve a copy of the letter which I wrote to the Minister of Justice. I presume that he files his correspondence and I think he will have the letter. If he has I would ask him in justice to mvself to produce the letter and read it to the House. I think I stated in the letter that I wrote that a member of the special committee to which the Bill had been referred had requested me to obtain from him his opinion as Minister of Justice as to the jurisdiction of this House in restricting the length of race meetings. At any rate, I remember well that I stated that in conversation to the Minister of Justice. Suppose I did not so speak. I wrote to the Minister of Justice and addressed him as Minister of Justice, and I should also say that the Minister of Justice knew well that I was chairman of the special committee having this matter in hand. Those are the facts and suppose those are the only facts; when I asked the Minister of Justice for his legal opinion, surely the letter I received in reply, not being marked ' personal,' or ' confidential,' was a letter that one might expect to 'use when he was doing what I was, and I would ask, if the opinions of the Minister of Justice, asked for by a member of the

House and given to a member of the House are to be treated as private correspondence, of what value are such opinions? I think I have reason to complain of the reference that the Minister of Justice made in the House. I wish that every statement the Minister of Justice had made to me when I consulted him about this Bill and discussed the Bill with him was, as is this letter, in writing and over his signature. I have a great deal to complain of, I think, as to the treatment of the Minister of Justice in connection with this whole matter. Having discussed.the question with him, as I have discussed it with him and he having made the statements that he did make, and which it would perhaps take too much of the time of the House to discuss, I do say that if I had used the Minister of Justice as he has used me in this matter, I would have thought that I had struck below the belt and that I had not acted either honestly or honourably. That is a plain statement to make, but if the Minister of Justice demands of me. to make the fullest possible detailed explanation of my words I am ready to do so at any time either in this House or outside of it.

speakeroldname: Hon. A. B. AYLESWORTH (Minister of Justice).
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have only to say that I regret more than I am able to express, the fact that I have not been able to hear what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Miller) has said, and I am sorrv indeed that he feels that he has any grievance or cause of complaint against me, either in regard to the letter he has referred to or in regard to anything I have said out of which this has arisen. I certainly had no idea of imputing to my hon. friend any dishonourable conduct in connection with the reading of the letter he has mentioned. I think the language which I used in speaking about it abundantly shows that no such idea was m my mind. I said at the time in the House that I certainly had no objection to his putting the letter on the pages of ' Hansard,' though I added that I never expected to see it there, nor did I. The hon. gentleman, being a personal friend, saw me repeatedly in friendly conversation in reference to the measure of which he had taken charge. I spoke to him freely with regard to the objects which he desired and I certainly never expected that anything which passed between us in those conversations would be matter of- discussion afterwards in public form. I regarded the letters which passed between us in precisely the same way. I did not consider-I do not consider now- that because I happen to be Minister of Justice I am in any way the legal adviser for the House as a whole or of any member of the House.
I am perfectly willing at any time to talk
with or write to any member of the House who thinks he can have any help from me in connection with any measure in which he is interested, or anything in respect of which he may apply to me. - It was precisely in that way that I understood my hon. friend was either speaking to me or writing to me in connection with this Bill, and all that I have said in reference to this letter is what I am repeating now, that while it was in no sense a private communication, while it was in no sense a breach of confidence that it should be made public, I did not expect that it would be. I was not upbraiding my hon. friend for the course he took, I was not complaining of it in any way.
I understand that my hon. friend has also spoken of the general course which has 'been taken with regard to the measure in which he is interested, as one in which he thinks I have done something unfair, or as he, as I understand, described it, ' struck below the belt.' I can only express my very great regret that any such feeling should he in the mind of my hon. friend, and I must also add some little astonishment, because during the few days which have passed since the occurrences of last week in the House, I have met miyyboni. friend' with 'quite the usual .cordiality which has always existed between us. it was the last idea in my mind that he had any feeling of being hurt with reference to the course of these proceedings. I should like simply to add that from the outset of this matter, from the opening of the session, in any conversations which had taken place between my hon. friend and myself, all of which have been of the most friendly-character, I have never concealed from him in any way that I was entirely opposed to the theory upon which the Bill he had introduced was framed. I have told him quite frankly from the outset that I very greatly preferred the English Bill. I thought that I was not doing any more than was fair to him in saying so, and I have in every way given him, I think perfectly clearly, to understand that I would not introduce such a Bill as the one which he introduced, that I did not approve of the scheme of the Bill, or the attempt which I thought it manifested to call the walking about taking bets the keeping of a betting house or place. That was a feature of the Bill which was essential to it, which was in a word the whole theory upon which it was framed. I regarded that as mere verbal trickery, and I certainly gave my hon. friend to understand thajt, as plainly I thought as any words I could use would enable me to do so. I think these circumstances that my hon. friend is scarcely justified in alluding to the opposition which I openly offered in the House to the mea-

sure which he had introduced, as in any way striking below the belt.

Just one word. When I obtained the views of the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Aylesworth) at any times I distinctly stated to him, at least on one occasion, that whatever opinions I received from him I asked and hoped to receive for the purpose and with the object of making use of those opinions of the hon. the Minister of Justice, and he did not say that he did not desire or wish me to do that, he simply said in reply that when the matter came up to be discussed in the House he would probably have something to say himself.
A word as to what the Minister of Justice has just said. His objection to the Bill was largely because it would interfere with private betting. The Minister of Justice said to me, when I was consulting him about the Bill, as I said before in the House, that it had been very carefully drawn by three clever lawyers, Mr. Raney, Mr. Cartwright of Toronto, and Sir Thomas Taylor, late Chief Justice of Manitoba. The minister said: These are three clever lawyers, they have given a great deal of attention to the drafting of the Bill, and I do not think it can be improved on, and the Minister of Justice said he added the words ' for the purpose for which it was intended,' and if he says he added those words I take it for granted that he did. But I took the care at times to tell the - Minister of iustice that it was not the desire of the promoters of the Bill to in any way interfere with private betting. Knowing that that was not the intention, he suggested that the Bill could not be improved upon for the purpose for which it was intended. I said to .the Minister of Justice: If this Bill, in your opinion, would affect the man who makes a private bet, I would like you to suggest any language that you can suggest that would leave out the private bettor and exempt him. He said: I cannot suggest any language that would be an improvement on the Bill as it is drawn in that respect. Afterwards I myself, fearing the Minister of Justice might make some further objections to the Bill in that regard, that is was interfering with private betting, drafted a clause and submitted it to him, and as he in his own writing amended it in order, as he thought, to fit the case. I said: Will the amendment, as you have changed it, fill the bill, and exempt the private better? He said: I think it will. The Minister of Justice then must have known that that was my intention. The Minister of Justice looked carefully over the Bill. He said that clause 235 did not in any way interfere with the private Mr. AYLESWORTH.
bettor, but that it would with the recording or registering of a private bet.
The hon. member understands that we cannot go over all this ground again. The hon. gentleman's present statement may bring about another statement from the Minister of Justice.
Do you not think the hon. gentleman should be allowed to explain himself after the mess he made of it the other night.

All I say is>
the Minister of Justice has advised me in one way when I consulted him, and has advised the House in an entirely different way.
Is it the intention to proceed with the Insurance Bill this session?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is the intention to proceed with the Bill.

I wish to ask the minister in charge of the Fisheries Department a question regarding Lac du Bonnet. I can perhaps, best do so by reading the following letter which I have received:
Lac du Bonnet, April 3.
Dear Sir,-Will you kindly give me some information regarding the Lac du Bonnet fisheries. It is rumoured that the Lac du Bonnet waters are thrown open for commercial fishing for the settlers and residents around Lac du Bonnet, which would be satisfactory to the people as long as the district is not invaded by Indians and foreign fishermen. There is a company preparing to buy the fish and they are telling us _ that they have bought the licenses and paid for them, and the settlers can get no license except through the company who wants an agreement signed which we do not think is right. If you could give ns some information in this matter you would do us a great favour.
Respectfully yours,

Lac du Bonnet, Manitoba.
I have had several letters to this effect. There is a company that has been trying very hard to .secure the control of Lac du Bonnet which the right hon. gentleman will remember was discussed before. The company, -I understand, have purchased a large number of these licenses from the fishery inspector at Selkirk, in the names, I presume, of settlers, and they come to the settler and say: We have a license here for you, and if you will sign an agreement to sell us the fish you catch under this license, we will give it to you. And they are going to the other settlers, and telling them that they cannot get a license except from them. Will the right hon. gentleman ascertain if

such licenses have been issued, to whom they have been issued, and to whom they have been handed? I would also ask him to see that the settlers, are protected in their rights.

House in committee on Bill (No. 115), to incorporate the St. Lawrence Power Transmission Company-Mr. Pardee.
On section 1, incorporation.
Have the promoters of the Bill looked over the amendments which have been suggested, and come to a conclusion?

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Yes, as stated on Friday night, we are quite content to accept the amendment suggested by the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden), and the hon. member for North Ontario (Mr. S. Sharpe). There is no objection to those amendments.

What about an amendment of which I gave notice, to enact as subclause 3 of this Bill clause 9 of the St. Lawrence Power, Company Bill? That is, re-enacting it so that the two companies would stand exactly on the same basis. It is somewhat more restrictive as regards the power of entering on property, it gives less extensive appropriation powers. Is the promoter of the Bill prepared to accept that?

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: I think that in so far as the acquiring of property by the transmission company for the transmission lines is concerned, it is amply guarded in the Bill now before the House, in this way that in the event of anything occurring they shall all come under the provisions of the Railway Act. There is a further provision that in acquiring either lands or easements it is absolutely necessary that they should acquire the fee simple. I think it is hardly fair to ask more onerous conditions, in fact I do not see how they could be imposed. Every interest is safeguarded thoroughly and absolutely. I would be quite content to accept the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Grey (Mr. Middlebro), it is practically the same amendment.

I have not given a great deal of attention to this Bili personally, but some hon. gentlemen on this side have come to me and made certain suggestions with regard to it. Another suggestion contained in an amendment was practically to this effect: This company is designed as I understand it according to the actual facts lor the purpose
of transmitting power which is produced by the St. Lawrence Power Company. The rates to be charged by this company are in effect made subject to the control of the Railway Commission of Canada. The St. Lawrence Power Company, however, was incorporated before we had any Railway Commission and its rates are not subject in any way to the Railway Commission of Canada. The difficulty which was suggested to me and which seems to me to have some importance was this: Suppose that the St. Lawrence Power Transmission company goes before the Railway Commission of Canada to have its rates fixed, it gets its power from the St. Lawrence Power Company; The St. Lawrence Power Company in dealing with the St. Lawrence Power Transmission Company says:	We	are
absolutely untrammelled by any control of the Railway Commission, we were incorporated before there was any Railway Commission. Then the St. Lawrence Power Transmission Company come before the Railwmy Commission of Canada and will say: We have been obliged to pay $25 or $35 or $40 per horse-power to the St. Lawrence Power Company. They are not subject to your control and we cannot do anything with them. Then the Railway Commission will have to say: You are subject to this condition of affairs: We cannot cut you below what you are paying, we must allow you what you are paying and something more and the net result wmuld be that there would be no effective control by the Railway Commission of Canada over the rates.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: As I understand there is no objection on the part of the promoters of the Bill to put in this Bill anything and everything that may be necessary in order to put as effectively as it can be put in the hands of the Railway Commission, the power to have control over its rates. I do not apprehend that the objection is a very strong one. If I understand the objection of my hon. friend it is not his own objection but an objection which was stated to him, and it is that there was some doubt as to whether the St. Lawrence Power Company, having been incorporated before the Railway Commission, would be made amenable to that commission. I do not think that the point is a strong one. We have created the commission and have provided that railway companies in existence 50 years before the creation of that board should have their tolls submitted to it. At all events, to make it doubly sure, I understand the promoter is quite willing to agree to the amendment suggested so as to clear that point and make it beyond doubt.
An amendment designed to cover that has been placed on the Votes and Proceedings of the 6th of April, page 796.
The promoter has agreed to accept that amendment.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would like the committee to consider whether in this private Bill affecting a power transmission line,' you can introduce an amendment affecting another company not under the view of this Bill, that is the St. Lawrence Power Company. I would like to have the opinion of the committee on that point. Whether this Bill affecting one company can properly be amended to affect the rights of an entirely different company by throwing on it duties not provided for in the notice given for the Bill before the committee.

I think it can be done in this case, for this reason. In the first place, parliament can refuse to accept the Bill unless this amendment be made. In the second place, there is the question of notice, which is the more important question. It is admitted, I understand, that the corporations, although distinct in form, are practically one. Therefore, the promoters of this Bill have the right, on behalf of the St. Lawrence Power Company, which they also represent, to come before parliament and say that they will accept the Bill with these amendments.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The point mentioned by the chairman is not so much a point of procedure as a point affecting our powers. As a point of procedure, if all parties have agreed to it, we can agree to it also.
On section 1, incorporation,

There are some other changes which I consider of a minor character to which I can refer as we go along. There is the one already referred to with regard to the curious change made with respect to the powers of expropriation. I refer to the use of the word 'easement'; and, of course, there may be other points of which I am not aware, because I have not given as much attention to the details of the Bill as have some other hon. gentlemen on this side of the House.
On section 6, powers,

It was suggested .that after the words, 'with similar lines in the United States for the purpose of importation,' the words, 'into Canada,' should be inserted. They were introduced in the Private Bills Committee, but have been omitted from the Bill as reprinted.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council

speechtext: I do not think that in a Canadian Bill the word 'importation' would mean anything but importation into Canada.
As the words 'United States' aire used there, might it not be construed as importation into the United States?

This parliament could not legislate in regard to importation into the United States. We can only deal with importation into Canada or exportation out of Canada. The object of this is to enable the company to bring in power from Wad-dington.
I am inclined to think that if there is no objection, the words 'into Canada' had better be inserted, though the word 'importation' probably means that.

The minister's statement that the object was to bring in power from Waddington hardly tallies with the statement of the Minister of Public Works, that in dealing with these gentlemen he would receive a guarantee that although 75 per cent of the power might be generated in the United States, one-half of it would be brought into Canada.
Would it not be stronger if the words ' to the company ' were omitted? That would cover the sale to any one.

I do not think you could very well do that in this Bill. There may be some excuse for putting it in this particular Bill, because it is said the two companies are composed of the same people, but I do not think that you could reasonably go further in this Bill than is already provided by this amendment.
If they should sell to another company, and that company should sell back, would they not evade the law?

The St. Lawrence Power Company is not brought under the Railway Act by this amendment, except for the sale of power to the St. Lawrence Power and Transmission Company. Why not bring it under the Railway Act for all purposes?

We should have to introduce a special Act.
On subsection 3; section 247 of the Railway Act shall apply to the works and undertaking of the company,
What is section 247?

I will read the opening lines of it, which will show the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) the general effect, and I will send him across the floor a copy of the Act that is before me:
When any company is empowered by special Act of the parliament of Canada to construct, operate and maintain lines of telegraph, or telephone, or for the conveyance of light, heat, power or electricity, the company may, with the consent of the municipal council or other authority having jurisdiction over any highway, square or other public place, enter thereon for the purpose of exercising the said powers, and as often as the company thinks proper, may break up and open any highway, square or other public place, subject, however, to the following provisions :
And so it goes on with the different subsections, covering, in all, two pages. But it begins with the provision that all should be subject to the consent of the municipality.

I do not understand that it says the consent of the municipality ' as expressed by by-law.' It i3 customary in the case of railway Bills, when we authorize the building of telephone and telegraph lines, to require that in building through municipalities all the work shall be done subject to the consent of the municipality as expressed by by-law. The municipality may then make conditions. I do not see why it would not be equally possible to do it in this case.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Subsection 5 of section 247 of the Railway Act covers that.

This subsection 3 of the Bill is the one I propose to strike out, substituting for it the section of which I have given notice. It is very long, and I shall not read it. But I may say that it is much on the lines of section 247 of the Railway Act, but it does not give the company as broad powers as are given under that section. But the amendment I propose is an exact copy of the provisions of the St. Lawrence Power Company Act, section 9. One matter in which it materially differs from section 247 of the Railway Act is in subsection (i) :
Nothing herein contained shall be deemed to authorize the company to enter upon any private property for the purpose of erecting, maintaining or repairing any of its works, without the previous assent of the owner or occupant of the property for the time being.
I do not propose to take up much time over this matter. But it seems to me that these two companies are so much one company that if they wanted an enlargement of their powers of expropriation they*ought to come to us fairly and openly and propose an amendment of their Bill. Thi3 is a test of good faith, and a very important one. If the company are acting in good faith, they ought to be prepared, I think to accept the provisions of the original Bill. They are substantially one company, carrying out the same object, the present Bill being designed to make provision regarding the transmission end of the scheme. I do not think we ought to expand their powers in any way, and thus give them a more valuable franchise than they have at the present time. I do not want to repeat what I said on Friday night. I wa3 sorry I had not time to complete what I then wished to say. I was endeavouring to point out that we ought not to put the company in a position in which, in case of need of expropriating their franchise rights, we should find those franchise rights enhanced in value.

have acceded practically to every amendment suggested, and we have it in such a condition that even those who were most strongly opposed to it in the Private Bills Committee and in the House are absolutely satisfied. Therefore, it is hardly consistent at this late stage to move that this paragraph be struck out.

Along the line of the argument raised by the hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Lennox), I may say that it was the intention of the hon. member for North Grey (Mr. Middlebro) to call attention to an Act similar in purpose adopted by the federal house at Washington. In addition to the fact brought out by the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Emmerson) that the state legislature of New York charged certain fees, it also provided that the federal Act should govern the Long Sault Bill, somewhat similarly as our Railway Act governs the railways, and I want to call attention to a most remarkable and very sweeping clause which these men are willing to accept on the other side. After setting forth that all the works will be constructed in accord with plans submitted to the Militia Office and Secretary of Trade and Commerce at Washington, and it is provided that these shall have absolute control, and the right shall be vested in the state and not in the company to regulate the flow of water, whether or not injurious to the company, and that at any future time the United States government may have this dam removed at once, either by blasting it or in any other way, if they consider that necessary in the interest of the government or navigation, and no claim can be made for damages or compensation of vested rights. That is a very broad clause which the company had to accept, and the reason I call attention to it is because it bears out the contention of my hon. friend from South Simcoe. It shows how valuable these franchises are considered by the nation to the south. As I read this Act. I feel more strongly than ever the necessity of our being very careful before granting franchises of this kind.

If my hon. friend were dealing with damming the St. Lawrence, the position he takes would be a wise one, but there is no question of that here. We have given other companies power to erect transmission lines throughout Canada, and in none have we insisted on any such provision. None of these is so restricted as the present company. If I were not very anxious to get transmission lines in order to obtain power in the vicinity where I live, I would advise the promoters to drop their Bill. If they were proposing to dam the St. Lawrence, that would be a reason for taking the precaution which the United States has taken, in case that should be found an interference to navigation, and Mr. PARDEE.
not give the company any claim for damages, but that is not the case here.

I have the statute referred to by the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Emmerson) in which he pointed out the very considerable fees charged by the United States for such rights as are here given. I need not refer to that further. I also have before me the Act passed by the House of Representatives, which provides that all the rights and privileges given under that Act are to be subject to an Act of Congress containing the provision referred to by my hon. friend from Kootenay. That will be found in the general statutes of the United States, vol. 34, page 386. It is entitled An Act to Regulate the Construction of Dams across Navigable waters. The Act of the State of New York is made subject to the provision of the Act I have referred to, among which are these clauses.
Whenever Congress shall authorize the construction of a lock or other structures for navigation purposes, in connection with such dams, the person owning such dam shall convey to the United States,_ free of cost, title to such land as may be required for such constructions and approaches, and shall j/rant to the United States a free use of waterpower for building and operating such constructions.
Section 2. That the right is hereby reserved to the United States to construct, maintain, and operate, in connection with any dam built under the provision of this Act, a suitable lock or locks, or any other structures for navigation purposes, and at all times to control the said dam and the level of the pool caused by said dam to such an extent as may be necessary to provide proper facilities for navigation.
Section 3. That the person, company or corporation building, maintaining or operating any dam and the pertiment works, under the provisions of this act, shall be liable to any damage that imay_ be Inflicted thereby upon private property, either by overflow or otherwise. The person owning or operating any such dam shall maintain, at their own expense, such lights and other signals thereon and such fishways as the Secretary of Commerce and Labour shall prescribe.
It also provides that:
Upon refusal of the persons owning or controlling any such dam and accessory works, to comply with any lawful order issued by the Secretary of War or the chief engineer in regard thereto, the Secretary of War or chief engineer may cause the removal of such dam and accessory works as an obstruction to navigation at the expense of the person owning or controlling such dam. and suit for such expense may be brought in the name of the United States against such person, and recovery had for such expense in any court of competent jurisdiction.
It also provides in section 7:
That the right to alter, amend or repeal this Act is hereby expressly reserved as to

any and all dams which may ibe constructed in accordance with this provision, and the United States shall incur no liability for the alteration, amendment or repeal thereof to the owner or owners or any other persons interested in any dam which shall have been constructed in accordance with this provision.
A general provision is thus running through the statute, enabling the United States government to have complete control over the works and remove them if necessary in the interests of navigation and without being under any obligation to pay any damages. Unfortunately we have nothing of the kind in our statutes. I refer to this so that at some future time we may be given the benefit of some such legislation.

In the absence of the hon. member for Grenville (Mr. Reid) I would call the attention of the committee to the fact that at page 704 of the Votes and Proceedings there is an amendment proposed by that hon. gentleman as follows:
Nothing in this Act contained shall he con strued to authorize the company to enter on take, or use any land or water, the .property of any province, without having first oh tamed by order in council of the Lieutenan Governor, the consent of the province t< such entry, taking or using.
As this Act has to do with the St. Lawrence Power Company, and the St. Lawrence Power Company have jurisdiction at the Long Sault rapids, Coteau, Cascades and the Cedars, I think it would be well that the provinces of Quebec and Ontario they having rights as to the bed of the river, should be consulted before any dam is constructed. I would, in the absence of the hon. member for Grenville, beg to move the amendment that I have read.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: I do not think this amendment should go into the Bill. If the amendments keep on, the company will not be able to do anything at all under the charter. I cannot see why this should go in. If we grant a charter we ought to grant a charter giving certain rights. We are not granting them a charter when we absolutely tie them up at the very first step they propose to take. If these people are entitled to come, and get a charter they are entitled to receive certain rights, and not a

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: That was when you thought they were going to build a dam.

The object of the amendment was to protect what the province claimed as its right to the bed of the river. That would only apply in case the Bill should give them authority to construct their dam. However, that question will not come up under this Bill.

I do not see that this parliament has any more power or right to incorporate a company with authority to expropriate the property of a province than a provincial legislature would have to incorporate a company with authority to expropriate the property of the Dominion. The Dominion is supreme within a certain limit. The province is supreme within a certain limit. I cannot see that any argument applies to one case that does not apply to the other case except it might be in matters of great national concern, .such as defence. The question of defence is expressly provided for in the British North America Act. The government of the Dominion has the right to take the property of a province for purposes of defence. But the British North America Act, in so far as express provisions are concerned, permits the taking of the property of the provinces for no other purpose. Apart from that the right would appear to be co-reia-tive. If the right exists in the case of the Dominion to expropriate it must exist in the right of the province. Mr. Chairman, when the earlier clauses of this Bill were being considered, I had not the advantage of being in the Hduse. The Bill has gone part-Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
ly through, but I would like to take the position now' that. I wrould have taken if I had been in the House when the first clause was reached. Perhaps it will be just as expeditiously proceeded with if I take the ground now that I intended to take, because the objections that are taken to this Bill were the same objections that were taken when the Bill was in the Railw'ay Committee. When the Bill was before the committee for a number of days, it was very fully discussed and was objected to as strenuously as the circumstances would permit. The Bill was amended very largely and some of the municipal objections-the objections by the city of Toronto-were removed. The principal objection that was taken w'as that the promoters who were asking for this Bill should have applied for whatever legislation they want to the Ontario assembly. The Bill is one that asks for a charter which is purely local in its character. The promoters are asking parliament to extend the powers contained in the original Act, being chapter 106 of the Act of 1906 of this House. This company was incorporated in 1906 under the chapter I have cited. The Act there gave the company power to construct a railway, properly speaking, from Hamilton to Waterloo, and another branch from Hamilton to Guelph, to be called the Hamilton, Waterloo and Guelph railway. By the Act, the undertaking of this company was declared to be a work for the general advantage of Canada. It was a purely inter-urban electric railway, which was given incorporation by this parliament. I desire to point out that four years have elapsed since the original Act was passed, and during those four years the powers conferred by parliament on this company have lapsed. The company have not carried out the requirements of the statute, and they are in the position of practically applying here for a new charter. I contend that they are in no better position than they would be were they applying here in the first instance, because they have lost whatever powers were given to them by their Act of incorporation. They have lost these powers because, of non-user of the powers, because they did not proceed, under the requirements of the Act, with the construction of the road. Not a rod of this railway has been constructed. It is contended by the promoters that a large amount of money has been spent in surveys and preliminaries of that nature. I am not aware whether that is so-I presume it is so-but even if it is so, the company has not, complied with the requirements of spending 15 per cent of the total cost in the construction and the commencement of the construction within two years, as mentioned in the original Act of incorporation. So that, they are here to-day asking for incorporation, and they are in the same position as if they

*were here for the first time. The objection I raised in the Railway Committee, and which I desire to raise now is that the matter is one of purely provincial concern, and that this is a railway that has its form, as it were, pointed out by the British North America Act. The sections of the Act are well known to hon. gentlemen present, and I shall just simply refer to them very shortly. Section 92 of the British North America Act, which contains exclusive powers of the provincial legislature, declares in subsection 10 that provincial jurisdiction shall be exercised with respect to;
Local works and undertakings other than such as are of the following classes:
(c) Such wrorks as, although wholly situate within the province, are before or after their execution declared by the parliament of Canada to be for the general advantage of Canada or for the advantage of two or more of the provincs.
This work, because it is declared to be for the general advantage of Canada is, _b,y virtue of our constitution, a Dominion undertaking. The effect of having it declared to be a work for the general advantage of Canada is, of course, to remove it from the provincial control and give it the status of a Dominion railway. What reason is there for it? It was argued on behalf of the promoters of the-Bill in the committee that these powers were essential. Some hon. gentlemen argued that because it crossed Dominion railways it should be declared to be a Dominion undertaking. That objection has long since been removed, if it ever existed in a case of this kind. Other hon. gentlemen urged, with regard to the handling of through traffic, that it was essential that it should be a Dominion railway and that it should be as such subject to the control of the Dominion Railway Commission. Section 8 of our own Railway Act removes both those objections. As hon. gentlemen will recollect, section 8 reads as follows:
Every railway, steam or electric street railway or tramway, the construction or operation of which is authorized by special Act of the legislature of any province, and which connects with or crosses or may hereafter connect with or cross any railway within the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada, shall, although not declared by parliament to be a work for the general advantage of Canada, be subject to the provisions of this Act relating to-
(a)	the connection or crossing of one railway or tramway with or by another, so far as concerns the aforesaid connection or crossing ;
(b)	the through traffic upon a railway or tramway and all matters appertaining thereto;
Both these reasons that were argued why it was necessary for this undertaking to receive Dominion incorporation are met, and provided for by section 8 of the Railway
Act which puts this railway, for these two purposes, under the control of the Railway Commission for Canada. This section 8 of the Act seems to have been enacted for the very purpose of meeting such cases as this. Otherwise there was no use in passing this. If short railways, railways that do not extend beyond the province or connect with a railway in a foreign country, are to be given incorporation here simply because they ask for it, what is the use of section 8? This section was surely passed for the purpose of allowing provincial railways to take provincial incorporation, and at the same time have the advantages of the Dominion Railway Board if they so desired. It has also been urged that for the purpose of financing a railway a Dominion charter was necessary, and while that may be so I desire to point out that if this were a provincial railway it would be governed by the Ontario Railway Act, as administered by the Ontario Railway Commission, and subject to all the advantages and restrictions of that Act. This- is in no sense a main highway of commerce. It is an electric railway, and as originally chartered it had power simply to construct from Hamilton to Waterloo, and from Hamilton to Guelph. Not a single foot of that railway has been constructed under that charter, and yet it now applies to this parliament for power to build a branch line from the city of Hamilton to the city of Toronto. So far as that new branch is concerned it is in the same position as if it were now applying for the first time for Dominion incorporation. That branch line is an entirely provincial concern, and in the respect that the most important feature of the Bill is with regard to its entrance into the city of Toronto, it is a municipal undertaking. It may be said that the interests of the city of Toronto are safeguarded, -and, while they may have been to a certain extent, yet to a large extent they are mot. This railway has not filed plans, it has not told the public how it is to enter the city, it has no route mapped out, and yet it gets a roving charter to come from the western limits of the city into the terminal station, and with certain rights of stopping at intervals, subject to the regulations of the Railway Commission. The provision for an entrance into Toronto is the feature of the Bill on which a fight was made in the Railway Commission, and as without that the Bill does not amount to anything, it is the feature which the promoters are anxious to retain. It was said in the committee that there was objection offered to railways entering Toronto, but that is not the case. The Toronto council make no objection to railways entering that city under proper conditions, but the people of Toronto certainly do believe that a railway should enter their city in a proper way, and that

plans and maps of the route should be filed, showing where highways are to be crossed, and how it is proposed to cross them. That certainly is a matter for the consent of the municipalities. This railway company has power to enter the city, and expropriate a right of way which is not delimited or* set down on plans, so that any one interested may know where it is going. The company has also the right to cross over, and under highways, and the Bill gives them power practically to force an entrance through the city in any way they may please. I would point out to the committee that this is at best a suburban railway, and that like other suburban electric railways it should be under the provincial railway board.
Is Hamilton a suburb of Toronto?
We hope some day that it may be.
Some day Toronto will be a suburb of the whole Niagara district.

The Toronto railway, the Mimico railway, the Metropolitan railway, the York Eadial railway, and the railway running out the Davenport road are at the present time all under provincial control, and they experience no hardship from that. There are many reasons why this road should be retained under provincial control. It is a street railway. True, it is not going on the highway, so we are told, but there is nothing in the Bill which gives us any guarantee as to that. Let us assume that they will expropriate their right of way through the country and still they are a suburban road, radiating some forty miles from Toronto through two counties. Why should not such a road be governed by the provincial law as are othpr railways of a like character? We are asking that this railway should be under provincial control, and that it should have the consent of the municipality before entering the city. What is the fight of this municipality to-day will be the fight of another municipality to-morrow. Our cities are growing, and the railways are radiating from the large centres of population, and if this parliament is going to declare that all these suburban roads are for the general advantage of Canada then the various provinces might just as well here,and now drop the idea of incorporating any railways, and providing regulations for them.
Let me point out that the local conditions of each province are made by local feelings, and local requirements. These are not Dominion matters. The environments of Toronto are not similar to those of Montreal or those of Winnipeg or those of Vancouver. The different provinces have the right, under the British North Mr. MACDONELL.
America Act, to create their own local authority in accordance with their own local requirements and local sentiments; and I ask if that is not reasonable. Otherwise, vdiat would be the use of giving them these powers? The people of one province know that what is good for them may not be good for the people of another province. Take, for instance, Sunday regulations. The province of Ontario has adopted the Sunday law. Other provinces may not choose to adopt it. They may desire to have their railways run on Sunday. The province of Ontario has adopted a law providing that any city having a population of over 50,000 can hold a plebiscite as to whether the cars may run on Sunday or not. That is a matter -which concerns local conditions entirely. I submit that all these local matters should be left to be worked out by local authority. Let me mention a few conditions of the Ontario Bailway Act which are not provided for in the Dominion Act-conditions that have arisen because of local requirements and local sentiments in the province. These conditions may not suit other provinces, but they suit the province of Ontario. It is set down in section 81 of the Ontario Eailway Law that a railway operated by electricity shall stop at such places in addition to those fixed by the company as the board may from time to time by resolution direct. They have power to fix additional stopping places if they desire,. Section 171 is a very important section, providing that fares to be taken by a company on a railway operated by electricity shall not exceed for each passenger five cents for any distance not exceeding three miles and for any excess two, cents per mile; and for each passenger under ten years, three cents for three miles, and for additional distance one-half fare. Subsection 2 of the same section provides that pupils under 17 years of age actually attending school shall be entitled to eight tickets for 25 cents. These rates have been enacted as fair charges for the carrying of passengers.
