I may say that that is one reason why I have raised objections to many of the charters we have dealt with respecting water rights and railway rights combined; while I felt that the railway rights would lapse by reason of non-performance of the work, the charter, so far as it affects water rights, would continue for ever, and might hamper people fifty or a hundred years hence, who would wish to use these water-powers. However, that i3 aside from the question. I wish to be particular on this point of jurisdiction, because on the next Bill on the order paper, I shall take the opposite view, perhaps, from that which I now express. I refer to the Bill relating to the Toronto Eastern Railway Company. I shall oppose that Bill.
It does not go through Halton.

I know the hon. member (Mr. Lennox) is joking. He will give me credit for better sense than that. The Bill with which we are now dealing has to do with a company whose work has been declared a work for the general advantage of Canada. But the Toronto Eastern railway, to my mind, is a road that, under the British North America Act, comes exclusively under provincial jurisdiction. I know that the Minister of Railways has expressed in the Railway Committee a Mr. HENDERSON.
different opinion, or, at least, the chairman announced a different opinion as being that of the minister. However, I am perfectly willing to disagree with him. This road coming into Toronto from the east does not cross any provincial boundary, nor does it connect with any other road that will take the jurisdiction away from the province. It has not yet been declared a work for the general advantage of Canada. It has been argued here today that it was a mistake to make this Hamilton-Waterloo road a work for the general advantage of Canada. Let us not make the same mistake with regard to the Toronto Eastern. I shall oppose that charter distinctly on the ground that the jurisdiction does not lie in this House, but in the legislature at Toronto. But the position in the case of the Hamilton and Waterloo road is that years ago it was declared a work for the general advantage of Canada, and, therefore, comes here properly for amendments to its charter, we being the only legislature having jurisdiction in the matter. I am sorry that the hon. gentleman should have moved that the committee rise. That would kill the Bill, on which a great deal of time has been spent and which would give us a very useful road. It may be said that I am somewhat prejudiced because the road is intended to pass through the county I have the honour to represent.
Are you any more prejudiced than Toronto?

I am not prejudiced at all. I am willing to give Toronto all the rights to which it is entitled. I want to help that city. I want to send its people the best vegetables and fruit produced in the county of Halton. We are willing to give them the best we have, but do not want to be compelled to send it to them in the most expensive way. What do you think the fruit growers of the township of Nelson, county of Halton, are doing? Hon. members may not be aware of the fact that this road has been constructed from Hamilton to Oakville, some 20 miles, and we want it continued into Toronto. Well, fruit growers in the southern part of the township of Nelson have actually loaded their fruit on the Hamilton radial railway, shipped it into Hamilton, and then transferred it to the Grand Trunk railway, in order to have it conveyed into Toronto. That is a round about and very expensive way. Whereas, if we had this road continued to Toronto these goods would go straight from the place of production into that city.
Hear, hear.

I am not so much concerned about passengers as about freight

traffic, but strange to say, all the discussion has taken place with reference to passenger traffic. Passengers can get into Toronto by means of the Grand Trunk railway or Canadian Pacific railway; but what we are more concerned with is getting our fruit and vegetables and other perishable freight into Toronto without the necessity of transhipment. By means of the radial railway, we could get them into the city at every hour of the day. The people of Toronto want our fruit and ' vegetables, and it is just such impediments as we are striving to remove which bring about the increased cost of living. These people are hurting themselves by making it more expensive than necessary to have produce brought into their city. We can supply them with all these goods they want, so that the benefit would be mutual. Do not, therefore, compel this company to build its line in the most expensive way simply because the Toronto Street railway might possibly lose a few fares. They talk about protecting their city, but I think this Bill amply protects it. Why, when this company gets to the boundary line, it cannot take on another passenger, and it cannot take on a passenger in Toronto at the terminus and let him off at any place in the city. It can only take him from the central part of the city and dump him out after it gets him outside. To my mind the street railway is amply protected. True, the city of Toronto 20 years ago made a bargain, and undoubtedly a good bargain, and leased to the Toronto Street railway the right to use its streets for 30 years. Some ten years have yet to expire, and the city is bound to protect its covenants or be liable to damages. I am not sure but that the city may yet see the propriety of making an arrangement with the street railway, paying it a bonus to extinguish that franchise and give over the whole thing, and then deal more generously with other railways coming into the city. I question whether the city of Toronto would not be the gainer if it "had more freedom to deal with new railways coming in, even at the loss of the $600,000 per year it now gets from the street railway company. I repeat that I regret very much the hon. gentleman should have moved that the committee rise. I am not going to vote to kill a Bill that I know would be of advantage to the people of my county, and which I believe will also be of advantage to the people of Toronto.

A few words on the interesting points raised in the discussion on this Bill. On the question of jurisdiction, from the facts stated here, primarily the local legislature ought to enjoy it, but we are unfortunately in the position that the Dominion government years ago granted a charter for this particular line. If the principle of law be as I understand it, 215i
once the Dominion government assumes jurisdiction, it cannot divest itself of that jurisdiction or vest it in the local government. My hon. friend from Grey (Mr. Sproule) will remember the argument used with reference to the School Bill, when the Dominion government was trying to vest in the local governments the jurisdiction vested in this parliament. Our argument was always that whatever power be vested in the Dominion parliament, that parliament cannot divest itself of. I think that the legal proposition is as clear as possible that if we pass an Act divesting ourselves of our power over this road, it will not reinvest it in the local government, and the local government cannot deal with it. Another nice question arises with reference to the duration of the life of a corporation. Several hon. gentlemen have argued that a corporation ceases if the conditions imposed by the charter are not complied with. We give a franchise to a company for the building of a road and it must be commenced within one year and finished within five. The argument is that if they did not commence operations within one year,' the charter lapsed. The old opinion -was that once you give an entity to a corporation it exists for ever. For a great many reasons it ought to be so. A corporation might incur liabilities, and if the corporation terminated with its failure to carry out its undertaking, you could not sue it or collect debt from it. The old principle is that once you give a corporation its entity, it exists for ever. I do not know anything about the merits of this road, but the question as raised by m,y hon. friend from South Toronto (Mr. Macdonell) is as to the proprietary right of the city of Toronto in all their local undertakings. I think they ought to have such a right for the benefit of the country, but it is a monstrous thing to say that we are precluded from giving a charter to a particular company because its railway ends in Toronto unless the company get the consent of the city to enter within its limits. If it invades any municipal rights let us make other provision for it. I think the Railway Act does make provision for such a case. The Railway Commission have power to impose such conditions as will fully guard every interest in the city of Toronto.

I would like to say one word in reference to what has been said by the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Hag-gart) with regard to the question of rights that we take in this parliament. My understanding of the British North America Act is that we cannot divest ourselves of any rights which are given to us and we cannot give to the province any rights other than what they enjoy under the provisions of that Act. But, I think we might claim rights that we would not be upheld in if

we went to the courts. We might assume lights and the courts might decide that we did not have those rights. I do not think we can claim a right because we assume it. I remember one time hearing the late Sir Oliver Mowat say: If I am in doubt as to whether we have the right to do a thing I go on, take authority under the law to do it, and let the courts decide whether we have the right or not. It is a kind of confiscation, but I do not think that taking a right would give us the right if the British North America Act did not in reality give it t'o us, and that we would be sustained by the courts.
The Privy Council have already decided the very opposite of the hon. gentleman's contention.
I would like to ask the hon. member who has the Bill in charge if the corporation, if this Act went through, could operate its road by any other power than electricity.
As I understand, it could not.

Well, I think the hon. member is right in that, because I do not see anything in the first Act which says it shall and in the second Act there is nothing at all said about it. In the Act of 1908 there is the following clause:
Section 10 of chapter 106 of the statutes of 1906, intituled, an Act to incorporate the Hamilton, Waterloo and Guelph Railway Company, is hereby amended by substituting for the word ' thousand ' in the second line thereof, the words ' seven thousand five hundred.'
That is only enlarging its borrowing powers, and it is the only thing that is in the Act; therefore there is nothing in the amending Act that would give it power nor is there anything in the Act which was originally passed. These -would seem strong additional reasons why this company should be under the control of the local legislature. The original Act says:
The company and its undertaking, shall be subject to such provisions of any general Act now or hereafter passed by the legislature of the province of Ontario as provide, in the interests of public health or safety, for the control and regulation of the transmission, distribution or supply of electricity in any form.
I do not know how it could carry out that portion of its charter with the declaration that this is a work for the general advantage of Canada. I do not see how it can be placed under the provisions of that Act and yet refrain from being under the control of the legislative assembly.
I wish to say a word with reference to the view put forward by the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Hag-gart). Of course, he is familiar with the Railway Act, and I do not suppose that he

has overlooked the section to which I wish to call his attention. This charter which was granted four years ago has not been renewal since, although an Act was obtained to amend the original Act for the purpose of giving the company additional bonding powers. Section 150 of the Railway Act says:
If the construction of the railway is not commenced and fifteen per centum of the amount of the canital stock is not expended thereon within two years after the passing of the Act authorizing the construction of the railway, or if the railway is not finished and put in operation within five years from the passing of such Act, then the powers granted by such Act, or by this Act, shall cease and he null and void as respects so much of the railway as then remains uncompleted.
The conditions of that section have not been fulfilled. Four years have gone and the railway has not expended 15 per cent of its capital upon the work. I do not say that the company has expired, but I say that the construction cannot be proceeded with under the charter. That is proved by the power that is sought by section 6 of the Bill now before the committee, in which the company asks that the time be extended during which it can do this work.
1 stated that while the power of doing what the Act authorized the corporation to do ceases, it does not affect the corporation.

It affects the question of their power to proceed.
Amendment (Mr. Macdonell) negatived, and Bill reported.
House in committee on. Bill (No. 116), to incorporate the Toronto Eastern Railway Company.-Mr. Fowke.

As the promoter of this Bill is not here, and as there will be a fight on it, I would suggest that the Bill be laid over. I therefore move that the committee rise, report progress, and ask leave to sit again.
I think the House is ready to go on with the Bill.
I do not think so. The custom of the House is that if the member in charge of a Bill is not here to look after it, and if it is a contentious Bill, it invariably goes over.

I think there is no particular reason Why we should not go on with the Bill, unless the powers of discussion have not been exhausted by the Hamilton and Guelph bill. I understood that the discussion was to take place on one or other of these Bills.

The hon. member does not want an all-night fight, does he?
M f. GRAHAM. The hon. gentleman should not make that remark. A threat of that kind does not influence me one iota -I am a sort of night hawk myself. That is really not the intelligent way to approach a question of this kind. We want to go on with the business, but if there is a strong objection on the part of hon. members to going on in the absence of the promotor, we might let the Bill stand over.
The Bill is just the same as the other Bill. Why not put it through? These gentlemen are only bluffing.

We are getting near the end of the session, but if every time a contentious Bill comes up hon. gentlemen ask that this be put off, we shall make very little progress. Let us go at it and dispose of it, unless a number of hon. gentlemen wish it to be put off. I am not pressing for one thing or the other, but I appeal to hon. gentlemen whether anything is gained by side-stepping the question.

I have taken objection to going on with a private Bill when the promoter is not present. As the minister says, however, we are getting near the end of the session, and we should not stop legislation for a reason of that, kind, although it is a very good one. I intend to oppose this Bill, but I would rather oppose it when the promoter is present, and therefore, it would suit me just as well if the Bill were laid over until he can be here.

Urould it be a fair arrangement to leave the Bill on the order paper "where it is, and let it stand until the hon. member in charge of it is here ? I want to do everything to expedite the business of the House.
No doubt the hon. gentleman will be here to-morrow, when after eight o'clock there will be an hour for private Bills.

There is no reason why we should not clear the order paper to-day of all the Bills except contentious Bills, and let them stand over. The business of the House has been much delayed by these contentious Bills, and if under the Rules of the House these were put automatically at the bottom of the list, or the rule of the British parliament were followed, and members balloted for the place a Bill occupied on the order paper at the beginning of the session, the business of the House would be expedited.

I would certainly object to this Bill being held over in order to let any other Bill take precedence of it. If there were any valid objection to this Bill, I would be found fighting against it; but I cannot understand why one gentleman supports one Bill and opposes another of the same character.

Had the hon. gentleman been in his place while we were putting through the other Bill he would have understood my reasons for supporting one and opposing the other. I am satisfied the premier quite understands it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do.

I think my hon. friend should withdraw the charge that I am inconsistent in supporting one and opposing the other. My grounds were well taken and are based on the British North America Act, and I am prepared to stand by the British North America Act, let the hon. gentleman diverge from it just as much as he likes to suit his convenience. I am going to stand by the constitution.
I did not hear the latest excuse that the hon. gentleman gives for supporting one and opposing the other, I am simply taking the case he gave in the Railway Committee that it runs through his county.

The hon. gentleman has no right to make that statement. Would parliamentary language permit it, I would say it was not true. The hon. gentleman did not hear that. Mr. Fowke, the hon. gentleman who is promoting the Bill now under discussion, threw out an insinuation that that was why I was opposnig it, and I immediately rose and repudiated the insinuation. I do remember some years ago stating that I was in favour of that Bill because it was for the general advantage of Halton. That is what I am here for. I am here to support legislation that is for the general advantage of Halton, and legislation in accordance with the constitution of the country, and I am opposed to legislation not in accordance with the constitution. The Hamilton Radial Bill is under Dominion jurisdiction and this Bill, to my mind, comes exclusively and entirely within provincial jurisdiction.

This Bill is going to be contested, and I think the rest of the time available for private Bills will be consumed in its discusson. I do not think it wise or fair that the minister should proceed with the Bill in the absence of the promoter.

Then the whole question I of private Bills should be set aside for

to-day, and some other business should be taken up because it would be a simple matter for gentlemen opposing the Bill to say that this should stand over and make it contentious to the end of the session. There should be no giving way unless the whole private Bill order is set aside for the day.

I think it is unfair that the House should be clubbed because this Bill happens to have a certain position on the order paper. There is other important legislation on the order paper and when a Bill is contentious the word of the Prime Minister is sufficient to make it stand over. To-day in his absence the Minister of Railways should have said it should stand. I cannot see why the hon. member should blame the hon. member for Halton for supporting one Bill and opposing another, because one railway goes through his riding. I cannot see why the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Hughes) interferes with railways in other people's constituencies. Neither of these railways touches his riding. The Prime Minister will recognize that necessity knows -no law in this matter; this Bill is going to he fought and it is as well that the member who has it in charge should be here.

After hearing the discussion my opinion is that this Bill is going to be fought for quitte a long while. If we are to close the session as proposed we have very little more time to discuss these Bills. If it is to be discussed why not go on and have the discussion. I think on the whole, in the interest of every one we might as well hear the arguments because we will hear no arguments on Thursday or Friday, so we had better go on with the Bill.
In the absence of the promoter, who would accede to any amendments?

The member came to me and some others, and he asked me to look after the Bill in his absence, and I am prepared to do so.
On section 1, incorporation.

I have to object to this Bill. Some of my objections are covered by those urged to the last Bill, and there are further arguments against it. The Bill in the first place does not pretend to qualify itself, so to speak, for appearance in this House under the constitution of the country. The railway is admittedly an electric railway, running between three or four counties, and not going anywhere within 100 miles of the limits of the province. The Bill in that aspect of the case is entirely a provincial Bill, entirely an inter-county or interurban Bill.
The hon. gentleman said this railway did not run within 100 mile3 of the border of the province?
Yes.
It runs to the lake shore.

Yes, and the American shore is 60 miles across, and the Minister of Railways might have some good ground for correcting me if the railway were to be constructed across the lake, which, of course, is impossible. There is no justification whatever for the presence of this Bill in this parliament. As originally drafted the Bill simply provided for the building of this railway to the limits of Toronto, but during its progress through the committee it thought it would like to get the same powers as had been given to the Hamilton, Waterloo and Berlin railway, and so the Bill was amended in that respect. In the case of the latter Bill, certain hon. gentlemen took the view that its prior incorporation by this parliament gave it a federal status which ought to be maintained, but the present railway has not even that excuse for seeking a federal charter. It was entirely an afterthought that this company asked for power to operate in the city of Toronto, and the provision to that effect was inserted in the Railway Committee. When the Bill met with opposition in the Railway Committee the promoters sought to give the railway an international character by stating that it was the intention of the company to run a ferry service across the lake, so as to connect with the New York roads, but in the Bill itself there is no right given to run any such ferry. That also was 'an afterthought.
How can you tell that?

There is no difficulty in telling that, because if it were the original intention of the company to operate a ferry it is reasonable to suppose that the promoters would have asked for that power. They might as well have left out reference to the Victoria-Haliburton branch, and then said afterwards that they desired to have it inserted. Why should the parliament of Canada give a franchise to anybody that asks for one. Why should this railway company be given running rights through the city of Toronto in face of the opposition of that city? Why should this parliament give to railway companies rights derogatory to the municipalities in the opinion of those who govern these municipalities. When the former Bill came before the Railway Committee the province of Ontario was represented by counsel, and in the name of the premier and on behalf of the government he contended

that this was purely a local undertaking, and he asked that this parliament should send the company back to the legislature of Ontario. The voice of the government of Ontario was heard, and it should have been listened to, and this company should not have been, in open defiance of the British North America Act, declared to be for the general advantage of Canada. Years ago it was an easy thing to have a work declared for the general advantage of Canada. It was given almost for the asking. But the right was not then regarded as of very great importance-certainly, not of the importance attached to it now. The people now are declaring against the improper use of this phrase, and are demanding that ' a work for the general advantage of Canada ' must be a work for the general advantage of Canada, or otherwise it is not to be so declared. I say, without fear of contradiction, that there is nothing in the British North America Act that justifies this railway in coming here; on the contrary there i3 everything in that Act to make it clear that it should go to the provincial authority of Ontario. If certain little railways are to be granted this right of being made Dominion roads by the mere exercise of our power, let us take down the bars altogether, and accord this privilege to anybody that comes here to ask for a railway charter, whether for an electric railway or any other. In that case, of course, provincial railway legislation, and the provincial railway commissions are useless. We ought to be consistent; there ought to be a line drawn somewhere; and if the line is to be drawn at all it will exclude such companies as this from coming to this parliament. For there can be no argument that I can see in support of these people coming here. I do not want to repeat what I tried to say on the Bill which preceded this, but I say that under section 8 of the Railway Act this railway has ample rights and powers to get the full benefit of the Railway Act of Canada. There is a reason for the company coming to this parliaments-there is no disguising that fact. That reason has been stated on the floor of this House on previous Bills, and the Teason is that a railway whose charter is got from the Dominion of Canada is more easily financed. I believe that to be the fact, and I believe that to be the reason why the railways come here. But what does that mean? It means that the obligations imposed upon railway corporations under the Railway Act of the province of Ontario are more onerous than those imposed by the Dominion Railway Act. For instance, there is the regulation as to fares, which, as I pointed out, in regard to the other Bill, oblige all railways incorporated by the Ontario authority to give cheap fares, special fares to children,
and to pupils attending school, and so on. Also, they are obliged to give protection to their motormen, and other workmen, give them certain periods of rest, choose them by examination which will assure their qualification for the work they are to do. Surely, these are public safeguards that the government of Canada should give heed to. But, in the case of a Dominion railway, the public have not the same safeguards. I submit, then, that the time has arrrived when the parliament of Canada shall decide whether the railways shall be favoured, or whether the people shall receive justice. Is this parliament to be guided by considerations of the benefit of corporations, or is the public to be considered, and due restrictions to be imposed? We seem to be clearly at the parting of the ways, and it is for this committee, and this House to decide upon its course. This railway company comes to this parliament because under our law the public will be left without certain protection that they would have if the charter were given by the province of Ontario. It seems to me that this is a fair way to put it, and that the position is unanswerable.
Much was made of the plea that the Railway Commission was the proper tribunal for the hearing of railway questions generally. But they have a railway commission in Ontario. We must assume that that commission will do its duty; we must assume that the province has appointed properly qualified commissioners who have due authority, and will exercise that authority for the public good. We find that very little attention is now paid to the cry of provincial rights. There was a time when conditions were different. I can well recollect the time, before the change of government in the province of Ontario, when my hon. friend the Minister of Railways . (Mr. Graham) was in the Ontario legislature. I believe the hon. minister was a member of that body in 1903.
He was.

The Liberal government of the province of that day objected, a3 its successor has objected since, to the parliament of Canada dealing, with these railway matters, and many other matters that come properly within the area of provincial jurisdiction. Perhaps the hon. minister (Mr. Graham) recollects a certain resolution passed in that House during the session of 1903. The provincial government became so impressed with the necessity of protecting provincial rights that they formulated a resolution, and sent it to "Ottawa, protesting against further encroachment by this parliament upon the provincial domain. That resolution will be found in the journals of the Legislative Assembly of Ontario for, 1903,

page 329. It was moved by Mr. Pattullo, seconded by Mr. Bowman-both ardent supporters of hon. gentlemen opposite- and resolved:
That this House protests against the tendency of late years on the part of the Dominion parliament in the matter of legislation whereby companies are being incorporated by special Acts, though such companies have purely provincial objects and come within the purview of subsections 11 and 16 of the British North America Act.
That the expedient which it has become customary to adopt of inserting in Bills the mere assertion ' that the works of the company being incorporated are declared to be for the general advantage of Canada/ afford no reasonable protection against encroachments upon provincial jurisdiction, the Bills being entertained and classed apparently in ordinary routine and without reference to any serious consideration of the question of jurisdiction.
That there is involved in this growing tendency toward encroachment on the provincial field of legislation and invasion of the rights of municipalities, which this House regards as of serious importance.
That the provincial laws relating to electric railways have been designed to safeguard in many respects the rights and interests of the municipalities through which these railways run or are chartered to be constructed, and the protection to municipalities thus afforded will be prejudicially affected, if not entirely removed, by the assumption and exercise of the right to legislate regarding these local railways on the part of the Dominion parliament.
This House, therefore, respectfully urges the Dominion parliament not to pass legislation of this nature pertaining to matters heretofore generally understood to be within provincial jurisdiction, and which, in their nature, are matters of purely local concern.
If that resolution had been drawn yesterday as a protest against this particular Act, it could not have been couched in more appropriate and pertinent language. That request was made by friends of hon. gentlemen opposite, and there it stands as true as when committed to print. If anything further were needed to emphasize the propriety and urgency of the resolution, I have quoted, it is what has taken place since. Time and again since then, this principle has been violated with the result that the province of Ontario has again and again sent down its duly accredited representatives to this House* to protest against the_ improper use of this term in cases of this kind. In this very case the Ontario government felt it incumbent to make this protest and sent its representatives here for that purpose.
