Committee resumed at eight o'clock.
When this Bill was before the committee much stress was laid

upon the fact that the incorporators of the company were men of means, substance and position in the locality. With that statement I entirely agree; I have nothing whatever but good words to say of the applicants for incorporation in regard to their status in the community. But, I submit with all diffidence that because that fact exists it is no reason why this House should grant these gentlemen incorporation in a case where it would not be proper to grant it to other people. The promoter of the Bill made the statement, I think, that any one of these gentlemen could build this road as easily as he could take his breakfast.
' Some ' of them.
There is tery little difference between ' any ' and ' some,' I think I am right in the statement I make all the same; however, I will accept 'some' of them.
Put it ' most ' of them, and you will be about right.

' Most ' of them. If that be so, if these people are of that calibre, if they are bona fide in their intention to prosecute this work, why should they object to curtailing the provision in this Bill permitting them to amalgamate with the Canadian Pacific railway, or Grand Trunk railway, the Oshawa Railway Company, the Canadian Northern Ontario Railway Company, or any of them? I protested in the committee against these powers of amalgamation with these powerful railway organizations, and I did so because this company, which is now seeking incorporation, is supposed to operate a purely electric railway of practically a local nature running between these counties'-an intercounty railway operated by electricity. If these parties are of the calibre that they are said to be, and I quite agree that those whom I know are men of means, and if they are going to build this road, then why need they be given such broad powers of amalgamation? These various railway companies that this company is given power to amalgamate with are to-day in the city of Toronto. They all have their rights of way to that -city, they all have whatever terminal facilities they require, and why should they be given this duplicate entrance into the city with certain powers, that, I submit, should not be given to them at all? That position was not met. There was no statement made as to why this railway sought power to form this amalgamation.
I object to this amalgamation upon the ground that a small railway company of this nature is given certain powers, and privileges that I submit would not be given to a large railway corporation. Just because it looks to me like a small undertak-

ing, and because it is apparently going to carry passenger traffic it is given certain powers. If this company amalgamates with and merges into one of the big railway companies, then one of these big railway corporations will have all the powers that this company has got under this Bill if it passes. I submit that this is not along the lines of prior legislation in this House. It would be an objectionaible measure upon that ground. That contention was not in any way met. This company has, at the eleventh hour, sought and received from the Railway Committee power to enter, and operate in the city of Toronto. If a railway is building throughout the west, through the most unsettled part of that country, or in any agricultural or Tural district, before the company comes down to Ottawa and appears before the Railway Committee it must be properly equipped with plans, and surveys showing its route. If that be so in the case of a rural district, I ask how much more should it be a requisite when a railway company proposes to enter a thickly populated, and large metropolitan city of the size of Toronto. Is there going to be one rule 'for certain applicants for railway charters, and a different Tule for certain other applicants? It looks very much as if that is to be the case. The hon. gentleman who promotes this Bill came here without any idea of having a local service in Toronto, and because he saw that a local service was being given to the Hamilton, Waterloo and Berlin rail-[DOT]way he, forsooth, thinks it very desirable to have, asks for it, and without either plan or route, or without showing how he is going, whether with a service underground or overhead, he is given this roving power to go at will through the city of Toronto from the eastern limit to a central station and even the central station is not mentioned. No location is fixed, no location is suggested. I do not think it is a proper way to treat this committee, or the House, or the locality in which it is proposed to operate in this blanket way. l7his railway is simply given blanket powers to enter the city of Toronto at will where it likes, and in the manner it likes without any limitation.

Is it not a fact that they cannot enter the city of Toronto unless they first get the approval of the engineer of the city, and if they cannot make an agreement, until they get the permission of a board of engineers? They cannot go in as they like, and they cannot locate a foot of this railway until the Minister of Railways approves of it, and they cannot go into the city until the Board of Railway Commissioners approve of it.
He knows all that.

I resent with emphasis the unfair statement of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hughes). He has made an unfair statement. He insinuates that I am making an argument that I do not believe in, and that is not sincere, and I ask him to withdraw the insinuation.
I reiterate with tenfold force what I said that if the hon. gentleman knows anything, he knows that everything he has stated here is not in accordance with the facts as stated in the Bill.
I ask the hon. gentleman to withdraw the statement.
I will make it again.
You will?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is a well known rule that every hon. gentleman in this House shall be credited with sincerity in anything that he says.
I did not doubt his sincerity.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman does not cast any doubt on the sincerity of the hon. member for South Toronto, then there is no question of order.

What I say is this, and I repeat it, that the statement which the hon. gentleman made, that this road enters Toronto at its own sweet will, without any control, is absolutely contrary to the fact, and he knows it, because he fought it out in the committee.
I ask you, Mr. Chairman, to compel the hon. gentleman to withdraw that statement, that I made a statement that was untrue to my knowledge.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is quite true, the rule prevents an hon. member from indicating that another hon. member has stated anything which he knows to he untrue. I have not gathered that meaning from the remarks of the hon. member for Victoria and Haliburton. It seems to me to be really more a dispute as to certain facts than any denial of an intention on the part of the hon. member for South Toronto to give the facts as he sees them.

I am simply taking the point of order on the words of the hon. member, who said that I had made a statement which was not true to my knowledge. That is unparliamentary and inaccurate, and I ask that it be withdrawn.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The statement put in the form in which the hon. member for Toronto puts it would be out of order, but I did not gather it in that form.
Then. I will continue where I was interrupted. It is quite true, as the Minister of Railways pointed

Jf the iteration of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Macdonell) that he thinks so and so where the British North America Act does not say so, I have no hesitation in saying that he has made out a very good case, but, unfortunately for him we have had just such railway charters passed by this House for a great many years. I received my political training under Sir John A. Macdonald, Sir John Abbott
You did not profit much by it.
Ii will compare favourably with that of the member for Toronto (Mr. Macdonell) I say that without hesitation..
You say lots of things without hesitation.

I had my training Isay under Sir John A. Macdonald, Sir John Abbott, Sir John Thompson, Sir Mackenzie Bowell and Sir Charles Tupper, and I shall read to the House a few of the names of the railway charters which were passed by this House when they were leaders, and which, by so doing, according to the logic of my hon. friend (Mr. Macdonell) parliament tore the British North America Act into shreds. Here are the names of a few purely provincial corporations that were incorporated in one year under the Conservative government: The Calgary Street railway, the Chilliwack Railway Company, British Columbia; the Columbia and Kootenay Railway Company, British Columbia; the Drummond County railway, province of Quebec; the London and Port Stanley railway, the Nakusp and Slocan railway; the Nelson and Fort Sheppard railway, British Columbia; the Western Counties Railway Company, Nova Scotia (a little one horse inter-county railway). These were passed in the old Conservative days and according to my hon. friend (Mr. Macdonell) the constitution was smashed. Then there was also the Yarmouth and Annapolis railway. Now, in another year there were incorporated by the Dominion parliament the following provincial railways:	The Windsor and
Annapolis railway, the Trail Creek and Golumbia railway, the South Shore Railway Company; the Shore Line Railway Company, New Brunswick; the Temiscou-ata railway, the St. Catharines and Niagara Railway Company (later on it became an international road); the Red Mountain Railway Company
That is international.

As a matter of fact the road was never built. The Quebec, Montmorency and Charlevois Railway Company, the Oshawa Railway Company (a little street railway running from the wharf up to the town). The Manitoba and South Eastern Railway Company, the Lindsay, Haliburton and Mattawa Railway Company (a purely inter-county railway), the Jamies Bay Railway Company, the Brant and Southwestern Railway Company, the Cariboo Railway Company, the Cobourg, Northumberland and Pacific Railway Company, the Dominion Atlantic Railway Company, the Edmonton Street Railway Company, the Erie and Huron Railway Company, the Gleichen, Beaver Lake and Alberta Railway Company, the Guelph Junction Railway Company and many others obtained their charters here, and bo it is in any year you choose, you will find any number of similar companies provincial in their character, obtaining their charters from this parliament. The examples I have cited were all under Conservative administration. Section 92 subsection 10-constitution of the British North America Act assigns to the Dominion of Canada

Suck works as, although wholly situate within the province, are before or after their execution declared by the parliament of Canada to be for the general advantage of Canada or for the advantage of two or more of the provinces.
There are many arguments in favour of all railways that purchase their own rights of way that run on a standard gauge no matter what the motive power may be, coming under Dominion jurisdiction. There should be for all such railways the same signals, the same rules, the same system of lighting and regulations, the same means of guarding the public. These should be uniform throughout Canada, and they can only be made uniform by having these roads declared for the general advantage of Canada.	,
I have taken pains to ascertain the feeling of the business men of Toronto since this obstruction has been going on in connection with the council or a few members of the council. I do not know whether they are all aspiring for public positions or further promotion, but I find that the leading business men outside of what you may pall the little municipal gentlemen are anxious to have all the roads enter that city they can get. They know what built up that city in the early days, they know it was the railwavs and they are anxious to have them there and they deplore the conduct of the council and representatives of that city in coming here to obstruct the Bill. They thought at first there was a desire on the part of the railway to run on the streets of the city, but when they found that was forbidden and that the road could not enter the city without first obtaining an agreement with the city engineer and then have

it come before the Dominion Board of Railway Commissioners, and that whether the Railway Commissioners approved or otherwise the company could not run along any street in Toronto without the permission of the board and the city, that they merely had the right of crossing the streets by overhead or underground crossings, and they must purchase the right of way. The council of the city of Toronto accepted the clause in this^Bill and the other Bill as satisfactory to them.
I rise to a point of order. The hon. gentleman is stating something that is not correct, is not true; the city of Toronto did not accept them.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That would not constitute a point of order. .
I contradict the hon. gentleman; I will not allow him to make a statement that is not correct.

I was present in the committee when the mayor and council agreed with the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Harris) on the clause that is in this Bill today. I appeal to the hon. member for Brant if the municipal representatives of Toronto did not accept the agreement about the entrance of the other railway into the city of Toronto on the same conditions as are here
I rise to state the facts.
I object to the hon. member taking the floor.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman can only interfere with the consent of the hon. gentleman who has the floor.

I will read the clause:
Unless with the consent of the city of Toronto, expressed by by-law, the railway of the company shall not be constructed upon or along any highway, as defined in the Railway Act, or easement acquired for public works in the said city east of Roncesvalles avenue, nor shall the railway of the company be constructed under, over or across any such highway or easement unless the plans and specifications thereof are approved by the engineer for the time being of the said city, or such engineer as may be appointed for that purpose, and the engineer for the time being of the company, and in the event of tlie said engineers failing to agree, by the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada.
Clauses 9 and 10 about carrying passengers in the city, I understand, are also similar in the. other Bill. Did not the mayor of Toronto or some representative oi the city of Toronto agree to those clauses in the other Bill?
I think that the member for Centre Toronto (Mr. Bristol) drafted that clause himself, and it was accepted by the sub-committee.	'
The hon. gentleman thinks.

Then I am stronger in my position that these clauses were accepted by the representative of Toronto, and the understanding I had was that these Bills would go through unopposed. The city of Toronto is properly guarded, no one of these railways can run along the streets without the absolute authority of the city. The Board of Railway Commissioners has not the option of saying whether it shall or not. It is the city of Toronto alone that can say whether the railway shall run along its streets or not. No greater protection can be afforded the city than is afforded by these measures. Several of the prominent business men of Toronto with whom I have conversed are very much opposed to any further or any factious opposition to these Bills, they want all the business they can get there. These are the men on whom the interests of the city depend and not alone the men in the council. Why do the city aldermen appeal for these restrictions? Look at Pittsburg today-a hundred aldermen indicted for bood-ling. Why should we place a railway entering the city of Toronto at the beck and nod of the aldermen there? Ought we not to protect the interests of the city? I contend that the Railway Commissioners of Canada should be the arbitrators in case the engineer of the city and the engineer of the railway fail to agree. The enterprise will be destroyed if left to the beck and nod of aldermen elected by fire-hall influence or anything else.

The inference drawn from the remarks of the hon. member will be that he intends a comparison between the hundred boodling aldermen of Pittsburg and the aldermen of Toronto, and it seems to me, that requires a little modification.
I think the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hughes) should be a little guarded in his remarks. There are many honourable men in the aldermanic body of the city of Toronto, and I do not think that the hon. member's way of speaking of them is fair.

I am obliged to ' the hon. member (Mr. J. A. Currie). But Toronto has fallen before and may fall again. Now, the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Macdonell) -objected to the powers of amalgamation given this road. Why, the Grand Trunk and the Canadian Pacific railway each have had power to amalgamate with other roads. The Grand Trunk has amalgamated with the Northern, with the Nipissing and with the Midland, and the Canadian Pacific railway has amalgamated with half a dozen roads around Toronto, and why should they be forbidden to amalgamate with this road or it with them? Why should this road be singled out for different treatment from that .accorded to

others? I have already given instances to show that, for generations back, this parliament, under Conservative or under Liberal rule, has passed, not one, but scores of charters for small railway companies. And the constitution of Canada is still intact. I must say that I could not understand the language of the hon. member when he told us that no plan of this road had been submitted. Why, there was a plan on the wall of the committee room which was referred to by the promoter of this Bill. That plan showed this road, its branches and terminals, all in detail. 1 wish to say, Sir, that the name of William Cowan standing at the head of this Bill- a man who practically owns two of the best banks of the Dominion of Canada-is of itself a guarantee that this Bill is worthy the best attention and consideration of the people of Canada and of this House of Commons.
Another very serious objection urged by the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Macdonell) was that there was no control over the rates for school children. Let me tell him that every morning children by the dozen travel on the Grand Trunk from points near Toronto, practically for nothing. Children travel to the Markham high school from both sides of that town. They get tickets at a rate so marvellously low- I think it is half a cent a mile, but I am not sure-that it is cheaper than walking would be. And, wherever they are wanted and wherever the trains run, suitable rates are made for school children. After the amendment of the hon. member for Centre Toronto (Mr. Bristol) which, certainly .was made with the consent of the mayor and the council added to the other Bill and to be added to this one. I must express myself as astonished at the opposition engendered to these measures.

My opposition to this Bill is simply on the point of jurisdiction. I contend that this company should have gone to the province of Ontario to seek a charter, as provided under the British North America Act. The hon. member for Victoria and Haliburton (Mr. Hughes) disagrees with that contention. I am not going to try to convince him any more than he need try to convince me that I am wrong. I will draw attention, however, to the statements which the hon. gentleman made with regard to the charters that were granted during the regime of the Conservative party to companies whose works were declared to be for the general advantage of Canada. It was quite impossible for one to follow the list as the hon. member read it. But I remember that he commenced by * mentioning the Calgary street railway, and , then referred to the Edmonton street railway, and to the Red Deer Valley road. Of course, he could name all the railways in
the Northwest that had received charters up to the year 1905, and say they were all obtained from this parliament, and that would be quite true.
How about the Guelph Junction, in your own county?

I remember very well that I had charge of an amendment to that Bill. It was a Bill to authorize the construction of a railway from the main line of the Canadian Pacific railway to the city of Guelph. But I was speaking on these roads in the Northwest. Where else could they have got their charter before legislatures were established in the western provinces?
I only named four.

I could not pretend to say how many the hon. member mentioned. But the names of those I do recall lead me to believe that, if the list were gone through, a good many cases would be found in which his argument was not well based after all. But, suppose that, in those days when less attention was paid to the rights of the provinces, such a thing was done, does that justify us in doing it to-day? I take a firm stand on that question. I do not want to see this trouble and difficulty that is looming up between the provinces and the Dominion perpetuated. I would .rather see peace and harmony. And to-day I think we ought to stand by the constitution as it is declared by the British North Amei'ica Act, attending to those railway matters that properly pertain to us, but leaving to the provinces those railway matters which are in the field of provincial jurisdiction. I do not propose to say anything with reference to the advantage or disadvantage to Toronto of this road being constructed or not. I am not interested in that point at all directly, but I have no doubt that there are people in Toronto who would be delighted to see that road get there, just as it appears there are others who do not wish to see it reach that city, because it will interfere with the arrangements made with the Toronto Street Railway. On that point I do not now express any opinion, but give my views purely on the constitutional ground.

There never was a time in our history when the question of transportation was so important as it is at present. Whatever is in the interest of the general transportation of the goods of the people or the people themselves, is to my mind to the general advantage of Canada. The time has gone by -when we can make a distinction between electricity and steam as a propelling power. It may only be a short time when railways will be run. across the peninsula of Ontario at any rate, by electricity, and that will not make them

provincial railways. There are large railways running to the city of New York by electricity and that does not make them local railways. It is not a question how railways are propelled, and I was surprised to hear the fact that railways are propelled by electricity used as an argument. The time may come when in this country the ruling propelling power will be electricity.

We are not there
yet,

We are getting there very fast and we are providing for the future. The question is such a large one, that we ought to view the case fairly, apart from provincial proclivities. I admit that, from every point of view, I am disposed to give the benefit of the doubt, whenever there be any, in favour of Dominion jurisdiction. Why? Because it is in the public interest that we should have uniformity of rates as far as possible, in every part of the country where our products are carried. This railway, it is said, ought to have a provincial charter because the British North America Act says so. I do not think it says anything of the kind. That Act points out certain railways which must be under Dominion jurisdiction, but it does not follow that these are all the railways which should be under that jurisdiction. The British North America Act points out others that might be under local jurisdiction, and evidently the men who framed it had in mind just such cases as we are dealing with now-because the Act provides that railways of an international character should have Dominion jurisdiction, and only those of a purely provincial character should have a provincial charter. But in addition, the framers of the British North America Act provided that if, in the opinion of the parliament of Canada, other works should be declared for the general advantage of Canada, they will fall, not under the jurisdiction of any one province, but of the Dominion, so that evidently the fathers of confederation had in mind just such works as the present. It does not seem to me the proper interpretation of the Act to insist that the Dominion jurisdiction must be confined to a few. individual cases since they left it open for this parliament to say what works outside these should be declared for the general advantage of Canada. Evidently it was their intention that we should give this parliament and members of its committees credit for dealing with these matters as men of intelligence, justice and fairness; and in that view they gave this parliament power to declare that any works, such as the one in question, are for the general advantage of Canada. This railway is evidently a work for carrying on the general transportation of the country.
Is that the meaning which the hon. minister puts on the words ' for the general advantage of Canada?-'
I do not suppose that the hon. minister desires to widen that term, because in that case an ordinary wagon road might be interpreted as being for the general advantage of Canada.

It might and it would be, if it ran the length of one province and into another, or even if it ran only the length of one province. But we must remember that wagon roads are usually the property of the municipal owners.
There are a couple of wagon roads for the general advantage of Canada to-day. One is the Monk road running from Ottawa westward.

My hon. friend asked me to state why I think this road is for the general advantage of Canada. Let me say that anything which will tend to develop or solve the transportation problem, which make the carriage of goods easier and cheaper, is for the general advantage of all the people. Suppose this road, as I think it will, should carry many thousands of tons of coal from Oshawa, that will be used in manufacturing goods that go to all parts of the Dominion, then the cheapening of the carriage of that coal is in the interests of trade and commerce and consequently for the general good of the people. Anything which will help to solve the transportation problem, and the general advantage of the people, and the framers of the British North America Act had evidently such works as this in mind when they made this proviso. My hon. friend from Toronto (Mr. Macdonell) says that this railway ought to be under provincial jurisdiction because all electric railways in that district are under such jurisdiction. He is wrong. The former government gave the Oshawa electric road a Dominion charter.

I said that the Toronto railway and all the railways running from Toronto within the limits of the province are under provincial jurisdiction, but the Oshawa railway is a road running two or three miles from the lake and connects with the Grand Trunk railway.

I understood my hon. friend to say that all the railways in the radius of this Bill were under a provincial charter; but if that point were well taken, then at least the portion of the line near Oshawa should come under Dominion jurisdiction. The question to me is whether this railway we are now discussing, is for the general good of the people. The Oshawa railway got such a charter because of its connection with the Grand Trunk railway.
Was not that the very xeason a Dominion charter was asked for?

The same reason would apply in this case because this railway asks the right to join with the Canadian Pacific, the Canadian Northern and Grand Trunk, and become a portion of these roads, so far as the delivery of freight is concerned. My hon. friend will not find a business man say anything else than that this railway is for the general advantage of trade and commerce, and that consequently it ought to come under the jurisdiction of the Board of Railway Commissioners. It is all very well to argue theoretically, but you cannot get a wholesale man .who will not say that any road going to the city of Toronto will be the better for coming under the Railway Board so far as its rates and operations are concerned. Toronto is a great distributing centre, and it is important that to and from the centre, goods should be carried cheaply for the benefit of the people. Just let me refer to the Osha-wa railway. At the present time the Osha-wa street railway carries the freight from the Grand Trunk by perhaps the most convenient way that any small electric railway in this country could do it. It has a Dominion charter, it has a connection with the Grand Trunk railway, and it delivers freight at the door of manufacturers in Oshawa and takes their freight from there to the Grand Trunk. I do not believe that there is a merchant, or any person who sells goods in Oshawa, who would ask that that road be disconnected and made what you might call a little jerk-water line by itself. I take a strong view on the question of provincial rights, and I say again that when it comes to the great question of transportation, cheap rates between one part of the country and another means cheap prices to the community and, therefore, it is for the general advantage of Canada, and I believe that the framers of the British North America Act anticipated just such an undertaking as this when they put that clause into the Act. As to the protection of municipalities, I say that ample protection is afforded to the city of Toronto by this Bill, and that when the Hamilton Radial Bill was passed to which the city of Toronto agreed, through their board of control, they gave greater privileges to that company than those which are given under this charter, and Toronto agreed to that only two years ago.
They had to.
Nothing of the kind. Does my hon. friend mean to say that the great, intelligent, broad-minded city of Toronto was compelled to agree to anything they found objectionable?

Yes, what could they do? The Bill would have passed without
those amendments if they had not agreed to them.

Does my hon. friend mean to say that even that would compel the big city of Toronto to agree to that which was wrong? This Bill will probably pass. Will my hon. friend say: I will not object because this Bill will pass? That would not be a satisfactory excuse to present to his constituents; neither is it a sufficient excuse for the city of Toronto agreeing to this other proposition. As a matter of fact, that company came to myself and asked for a charter. I told them that they could not get that charter through in that shape, and that they could not get it through unless they agreed with the city of Toronto. They went to Toronto and came back with a signed agreement from the representatives of the city, and the city gave more to the Hamilton Radial Railway 'Company than we are going to allow this company as far as concessions are concerned. The city of Toronto is fully protected. In the first place, the railway cannot be located for 100 yards without the consent of'the Minister of Railways. The plans and profiles of the whole line of the railway must be approved. Then, further than that, when it comes to be finally located the company cannot proceed with the construction of one mile of their line without the consent of the Board of Railway Commissioners. That is all protected. Are we prepared to do away altogether with responsible government? Is my hon. friend prepared to say that no government can do this business properly? He cannot say that, because the people and this parliament say otherwise. In addition to that they had the protection of the Board of Railway Commissioners. The commissioners settle where and how they enter the city of Toronto. They cannot go in where they like or how they like. There are special conditions that exist in Toronto that do not exist in smaller municipalities. I am prepared to frankly admit that every protection should be afforded, and I believe that such protection should be provided. The company cannot cross a street, above, below or on the level, and that means that they cannot get in at all, because they will encounter a street as soon as they get to the limit of the city, without first obtaining the consent of the city engineer.
Not a crossing of the street.
The engineer of the city of Toronto and the company must agree.
Not as to the crossing of a street.. That may be if they want to go underneath or above, but not in crossing.
They cannot get in anyway. They cannot get in unless they agree, and if they do not agree, then the Railway Commissioners must approve.
Suppose they will not agree, what happens?

Supposing they do not, they are in the position that every other city in Canada is in. I say that the amendment was agreed to by the representatives of the city of Toronto in the committee. Let me say frankly that I would rather, were I fighting for the city of Toronto, have the protection of the Railway Commission under the Act than any section as to an agreement between the engineer of the city of Toronto, and the company. Only a short time ago the city of Ottawa agreed with the Canadian Northern Railway company to certain level crossings, but the Board of Railway Commissioners refused to ratify the agreement between them and the city. While consenting that this clause should go in for the better protection of the city of Toronto I submit that Toronto is not as well protected as it would be if it relied upon the Board of Railway Commissioners. Every safeguard that any municipality could desire, every safeguard that the city of Toronto could think of, practically, has been put into this Bill, and there is no reason, to my mind, unless we simply take the ground that we are not going to allow any railways to be constructed where anybody objects to them, why this Bill should not become law because no provincial rights are infringed, and every right of every municipality is fully protected by the amendment.
I just want to correct a few impressions that the minister has created. The minister has stated that the representatives of Toronto agreed to this Bill.
I say so now.

That is not correct. What was done is this, the same as was done in connection with the Hamilton Radial Bill. For days and days, this Bill was debated in the Railway Committee, and several votes had been taken on minor portions of the Bill. The Bill was not passed, but it became self-evident that it would pass in a most obnoxious form unless the city made some concession. They did not agree to what was put in the Bill, but they accepted it as Hobson's choice. It was the best they could get, they had to take it or nothing, and so it is that this Bill comes to this House in this shape. The section that was spoken of by the minister, and other hon. gentlemen to-night as having been drawn by Mr. Bristol was referred to a Select Committee of which Mr. Bristol was a member, and that committee reported this amendment back to the House. I was not present at the meeting, and I do not know who was at the committee, but it was the best that could be got at the time by the representatives of the city.
Did they not agree to it?
No
Yes, excuse me they did agree to it.
What do1 you mean by agreeing to it?
The representatives of the city of Toronto agreed to that clause.
Agreed to take the best they could get.
Nonsense.

I want to place before the committee the following telegram from Mayor Geary in reference to this Bill. It is dated April 5, and was sent when the Bill appeared on the order paper last week: Toronto, Ontario, April 5, 1910. Claude Macdonell, M.P.,
House of Commons,
Ottawa.
You may state in the House that Hon. Sir James Whitney and his government are strongly opposed to the granting of the proposed Toronto Eastern Railway charter.
(Sgd.) G. R. GEARY,
Mayor.
So that Toronto does object to it. It is the best they could get.

It is well that there should not be any mistake about-this. We spent weeks upon this Bill. When this amendment came back from the special committee I asked the gentlemen representing both sides: Is this amendment agreed to? This is not second hand. They both said to me: Yes, if this goes through there will be no objection, they handed in the amendment, and it went through. If you can call anything an agreement I would say that that was one.

It seems that that agreement is very much like it might be supposing the minister was condemned to be hanged. If he were asked if there was not some more humane death and some one suggested bleeding him to death, he would accept what he regarded as the easiest mode of dying because he was going to be killed anyway. It is very much on the same principle that the mayor of Toronto and the hon. members representing that city accepted these provisions, because they could not get any better. I am opposed to this Bill in the first place because the province has strenuously objected to interference with provincial rights. We are provoking the antagonism of the provinces by our invasion of provincial rights with regard to water-powers and chartering provincial railways and in many other directions, and that feeling of ill will is bound to grow until ultimately it may cause us a great deal

of trouble. We should dp everything possible to avert such a condition of things. The hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Hughes) cited a number of charters of a similar character to this which were granted by this parliament when the Conservatives were in power, but the fact is that in the early history of confederation very few people objected to the federal parliament granting these charters. The only province for many years after 1878, that protested against our granting charters to institutions of this kind was the province of Quebec. I then thought that these objections were fairly good, and it was a surprise to me that so little heed was paid them by the federal parliament. We did not then appreciate the full intent of the clause of the British North America Act which referred to a work being for the general advantage of Canada. For a long time we regarded that as a mere formal thing, but our ablest lawyers have come to conclude that these words must have had some substantial reason at the back of them. The Minister of Railways has to-nighjt given a very strong argument for declaring a work to be for the general advantage of Canada when he said that such a work should be in the interest of trade and commerce, or in the interest of the transportation of the produce of the country generally. Another strong argument is that they might be applied in regard to the legal status of those who tried to secure their rights against common carriers who handle the produce of the country generally. But, let me give an example of what I think would be a very strong reason for incorporating a provincial undertaking under the declaration that it was for the general advantage of Canada. Suppose the Canadian Pacific railway reaches Toronto from the east and the Canadian Northern reaches Toronto from the west, and authority is sought to build a line to connect these two railways so as to make them one continuous transportation route, we might fairly say that the connecting line was for the general advantage of Canada; but, in the case of a short railway entirely within a province which does not connect with other transportation lines there is no justification for saying that it is a work for the general advantage of Canada. Whether right or wrong that is the view I entertain. Now, the hon. member (Mr. Hughes) told us that the fact that Mr. William Cowan, a man who. owns two banks was at the head of this railway ought to be a guarantee that it is all right. Well, he might have told us that Rock-feller of the oil trust is at the head of a railway but that would be no argument to me. The very fact that a man is wealthy , 216
may enable him to build the railway, but at the same time it may make him a power for evil instead of a power for good. We all know that many of these rich corporations and rich men exercise the power of their wealth not for the good of the people but to their detriment. I repeat that the exceptional condition in the city of Toronto justifies the city having exceptional control over railways proposing to build their lines through the city. Then, as to the railways mentioned by the hon. member (Mr. Hughes) as having obtained their incorporation from the federal parliament under the Conservative regime, such railways as the Calgary railway and the Edmonton railway had to come here because then there were no provincial legislatures in these provinces, and many of the others mentioned were extensions of the Canadian Pacific railway which being chartered by this parliament, the branches had to come here for incorporation also. But, the line which we are now asked to incorporate is not connected with any of the great transportation, transcontinental or interprovincial lines. It is merely a local railway which may take freight from the Canadian Northern railway or the Canadian Pacific railway and charge an extra freight rate for hauling it a short distance. They may do as some of the railways are doing to-day, pick up a car at West Toronto and take it to Leaside, and charge for handling it as much as a railway will for taking a car a hundred miles, because it is on another line. The Railway Commission should have some control over this company, but that does not afford a strong argument why it should get its corporate powers from this parliament unless it is connected with other railways.

I do not wish to delay the House in the consideration of this Bill, but I would, like to offer a few remarks on some of the issues which have been raised to-night in connection with it. The first issue has been raised by the hon. member for Victoria and Haliburton (Mr. Hughes), who says that a great many charters for small railways throughout the country have been granted by Conservative governments, and possibly by Liberal governments in the past. Any one who knows the history of railway legislation in this country knows that the words ' for the general advantage of Canada ' have been inserted in railway charters granted by this parliament, so that the railways might be able to secure the government subsidy of $3,200 a mile which was granted by the Dominion government. The most recent case in point is that of the Ontario government railway, which was built from the town of North Bay as



far north as Cochrane, a colonization road in every sense of the word. Application was made to this government by the legislature of Ontario for the customary subsidy, but it was refused. Now, I understand that the policy of parliament is not to grant subsidies to railways in the thickly settled parts of the country; and in those sections electric railways are taking the place of steam railways. For a long time the charters for these electric or traction railways were granted by the provincial legislature. I can remember a great outcry which was raised in the province of Ontario, when the Minister of Railways wa3 a minister in the provincial government, and when charter mon-gering became a scandal; and it was chiefly for that reason that the people of Ontario put out the Reform government there. It was whispered that it would not be many years before the applications for these charters were made to this House, and we now find that to be the case more and more every day. For my part, as a Conservative who wishes to see a change of government in this country, the more charters of that kind that are granted the more it will be for the advantage of the Conservative party. The mere fact that one or two members on this side of the House are in favour of a particular charter does not indicate that the Conservative party are in favour of the granting of these charters. The Minister of Railways states that the city of Toronto is satisfied with the amendment proposed. I asked the mayor and the city solicitor of Toronto, on their way home from attending the Railway Committee, if it suited them, and their reply was that it was the best they could get, but that they were not satisfied with it, and that statement is borne out by the telegram which the hon. member for South Toronto has read. The Minister of Railways is very strong in regard to the control of rates. Let me tell him that a great many industrial institutions have been established in towns and villages_ of the province on the distinct understanding that certain specified rates should be given to them by the railways in order that they might compete with similar institutions in the city of Toronto. But what do we findi? We find that they enjoyed those rates for many years; but as soon as the Railway Commission was established the railways took advantage of it to compel the people of those towns and villages to pay the same rates as they did before those agreements were made.
Would not that come under the statute which provides against discrimination?

The hon. minister must bear in mind that there are certain points such as Newmarket, which have to M. J. A. CURRIE.
compete with the city of Toronto, though they have not the same advantage of competitive rates, and they are at a disadvantage under the regulations of the Railway Commission. In this respect the regulations of the commission have not inured to the advantages of towns and villages scattered throughout the provinces, which are on only one line of railway. Another point I wish to bring to the attention of the House is that this matter is left entirely to the engineer of the city of Toronto, and if he, and the company disagree, it goes to the Railway Commission. The hon. member for Victoria and Hali-burton (Mr. Hughes) says he does not believe in placing any company at the mercy of a band of aldermen such as those in Toronto. I would rather trust the rights of the people to a dozen or half-a-dozen men, than to one man; but from the point of view of the company I admit that _ it would be more advantageous to deal with one man than with a dozen. If there is to be any dealings with the city of Toronto, it should be with the city council, and not with the engineer. The hon. member (Mr. Hughes) should consider seriously this question from the standpoint of public and provincial rights. I think this House would be justified in rejecting this Bill because it is a vicious measure in principle, the public are not in favour of it, and if the Minister of Railways thinks the city of Toronto would justify him in it, I am sure the member for South Toronto (Mr. A. C. Macdonell) would be prepared to meet him there at any time, and discuss the question before the electors. I am sure if he were to discuss it he would have a warm welcome.

It is to be regretted that the Minister of Railways on behalf of the government has not made a frank declaration of the policy of the government, namely, that it is to abolish the distinction entirely between provincial and Dominion rights in reference to the granting of railway charters. If they will say that they will give charters to any company asking for them it will save a great deal of time. We have devoted much time to discussing the question of provincial rights in this connection within the last two sessions, and I do not remember one case in which the government has refused to grant a charter on the ground that the province had a right to deal with the matter. Every argument advanced by the minister in favour of this charter would be just as applicable to an application to this parliament for a charter to run a street railway in the city of Toronto because large merchants in Toronto live three or four miles out of the city, and it is important that they should get to their offices early in the morning. I suppose in one sense an indus-

trious old lady who keeps a cabbage garde/i is carrying on an industry for the general advantage of Canada. Where the British North America Act gives jurisdiction to grant charters under certain circumstances, it must be implied that there are some cases where provincial governments have the right to grant charters. I would like the minister to give a case where this government could not grant a charter on the ground of provincial rights. It -would be a great saving of time if the government would announce its policy in this matter.

The hon. member for Haliburton (Mr. Hughes) asked me a question which I neglected to answer. I enumerated a certain number of railways, such as the Calgary street railway and the Edmonton street railway, that were chartered by this parliament and said also that throughout the western provinces there was no other parliament to charter railways. The hon. member put the question: What about the Guelph Junction railway? I do not know if he had in mind that I had charge of a Bill in the late eighties amending that charter, and had discovered that I had permitted the passing of the Bill declaring that to be for the general advantage of Canada when it did not come within the jurisdiction. The original Guelph Junction Act was passed in 1884 and the Bill to which I referred was an amendment. The Railway Act at the time provided as follows :
The Intercolonial railway, the Grand Trunk railway, the North Shore railway, the Northern railway, the Hamilton and Northwestern railway, the Canada Southern railway, the Great Western railway, the Credit Valley railway, the Ontario and' Quebec railway and the Canadian Pacific railway are hereby declared to be works for the general advantage of Canada, and each and every branch line or railway now or hereafter connecting with or crossing the said lines of railways or any of them, is a work for the general advantage of Canada.
The Guelph Junction railway connects with the old Credit Valley railway and consequently I was right in promoting that Bill and having incorporated in it a clause that it is for the general advantage of Canada. I admit that the law has been changed since, and that the connection would now only make it a work for the general advantage of Canada so far as the point of contact was concerned, but at that time the law was different. Mr. FIELDING moved that the House go into committee to-morrow to consider the following proposed resolution:
1. Resolved, that it is expedient to provide that the Minister of Finance be authorized to pay out of the consolidated revenue fund of Canada, for the purposes hereinafter referred to, in addition to the sums authorized to be paid under the provisions of chanter 10 of the Acts of 1899, an Act respecting the city of Ottawa, and amending Act, chapter 45 of the Acts of 1903, the sum of forty thousand dollars annually, for a period of ten' years from the first day of July, 1909, making a total annual payment during said period of one hundred thousand dollars; such additional sums to be paid into a chartered bank to be designated by the minister, to the credit of the Ottawa Improvement Commission, and to be by the commission expended for all or any of the purposes for which the commission is authorized by section 7 of said chapter 10, to expend sums placed at its credit.
. 2. That the Minister of Finance be authorized to pay out of the consolidated revenue fund to the corporation of the city of Ottawa, as a contribution to the maintenance of the fire protection service of the corporation, the sum of fifteen thousand dollars annually for a period of ten years from the first day of July, 1909, the first of such payments to be made as soon as may be after the passing of any Act founded on these resolutions, and the remaining nine annual payments to be payable in advance during the month of July in each year, the last payment to be made in the month of July, 1918.
He said: His Excellency the Governor General having been acquainted with the subject matter of this resolution recommends it to the consideration of the House.
Motion agreed to.
